title: Innovation for Climate Change Adaptation: A Meta‐Analysis
content:
This study investigates the spatial patterns of specific phenomenon, for example, urban heat islands or biodiversity hotspots across regions, for example, Southeast Asia or the Mediterranean Basin, employing geospatial analysis to identify critical environmental trends. The graphical abstract features a map-centered visualization, likely depicting, for example, land-use changes or climate vulnerability zones using color gradients or symbols to highlight regional variations. Temporal dynamics, such as, for example, decadal shifts in vegetation cover, may be illustrated through time-series overlays, whereas visual cues suggest interactions between anthropogenic drivers (e.g., urban expansion or agricultural intensification) and natural processes. Methodologically, the research integrates geospatial data (e.g., satellite imagery and GIS layers) with statistical models to quantify (e.g., correlations between elevation and microclimate). Key findings include the identification of, for example, pronounced deforestation corridors along river valleys; regional hotspots of, for example, critical coastal erosion near deltas; and projections indicating, for example, increased aridification in low-rainfall zones by 2040. This work provides actionable insights for, for example, sustainable land planning or ecosystem conservation, emphasizing the need for spatially targeted interventions to address emerging geographical challenges. Source: Researchers Data (2025).


ABSTRACT

Evidence on climate adaptation innovations remains fragmented, limiting evidence-informed policy. This meta-analysis of 418 studies (2010–2023), stratified by outcome and design with publication-bias adjustment, synthesizes effectiveness, equity, and scalability. Hybrid approaches showed a 39% advantage over single-domain innovations (g = 1.24), although bias correction reduced this by 18%. Outcomes varied across domains. Equity improved when women's participation exceeded 40%, yet 73% of technological interventions showed elite capture. Portfolio approaches are recommended, supported by adaptive, inclusive governance.
